input.title: Why coffee makes you crash
input.viewerQuestion: If caffeine wakes you up, why do you feel so tired a few hours later?
input.audience: People who rely on coffee to get through the afternoon

sections.heading: Opening hook
sections.purpose: Show a specific audience problem, immediate visual promise and central question.
sections.text: You drink a coffee at nine and feel sharp. By one o'clock you can barely keep your eyes open. The coffee did not give you energy. So what did it actually do?

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.purpose: Establish relatable stakes, baseline and scope without repeating the hook.
sections.text: All morning your brain builds up a chemical called adenosine. The more of it you have, the sleepier you feel. Think of it as pressure that keeps rising until you sleep.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.purpose: Explain the causal mechanism with sourced examples, not a generic list.
sections.text: Caffeine looks enough like adenosine to sit in the same receptors. It blocks the signal, but it does not remove the chemical. The pressure keeps building behind the block.

sections.heading: What changes the outcome
sections.purpose: Compare options, sensitivity or useful next steps with limitations.
sections.text: When the caffeine wears off, everything that was waiting arrives at once. That is the crash. Waiting ninety minutes after you wake up lets the first wave clear, and a short walk helps more than a second cup.

sections.heading: Answer and takeaway
sections.purpose: Resolve the opening question and make the caveats explicit.
sections.text: So coffee never gave you energy. It borrowed time from later in the day. Use it for that, and plan for the moment the loan comes due.
